<div class="project-hero-meta"><span class="type-pill">Methodological research</span><span class="status-pill">Ongoing</span></div>

## Overview

I am developing extensions of regression-based multiple imputation for studies that contain both scalar measurements and functional observations such as neuroimaging or EEG trajectories. The work adds a functional-principal-components-regression approach for imputing missing scalar variables within the fregMICE framework, evaluates the method through large-scale simulation, and applies the workflow to multimodal clinical and EEG data.

## Research problem

Complete-case analysis can discard substantial information when high-cost multimodal data are incomplete. Existing multiple-imputation practice is mature for scalar data, but mixed missingness across functional and scalar variables creates additional modeling and uncertainty challenges.

## Why it matters

Biomedical studies increasingly collect densely measured functions alongside demographic, treatment, and clinical variables. An imputation strategy that uses both information types may reduce information loss while respecting uncertainty—provided its performance and limitations are evaluated carefully.

## My contribution

I developed the functional-principal-components-based extension, designed and implemented the simulation study, ran reproducible large-scale evaluations on GW's Pegasus high-performance computing environment, and applied the workflow to multimodal clinical and EEG data. I presented the simulation work at GWSPH Research Day 2026 and contributed to the JSM 2026 paper.

## Data and study design

The methodological evaluation includes samples of 100 and 350 under 10%, 20%, and 30% missingness, with scalar-only and mixed-missingness scenarios and both smoother and bumpier functional settings. The developing workflow is also being applied to multimodal clinical and EEG data from a major-depressive-disorder study.

## Statistical methods

- Functional regression multiple imputation by chained equations (fregMICE)
- FPCR- and penalized-functional-regression approaches for missing scalar variables
- Penalized function-on-function regression for missing functional responses
- Rubin's-rule pooling and comparison of alternative covariance estimators
- Simulation evaluation using bias, error, coverage, interval width, and computation time

## Results and practical contribution

The approved poster reports that the functional-regression imputation approaches generally tracked the simulated targets more closely than complete-case analysis. Performance became more difficult at higher missingness and near complex functional features, and interval performance was sensitive to the covariance estimator. The real-data application extends the work beyond the poster's simulation-only time point; application-specific results are not summarized here before final review.

## Limitations

Simulation scenarios necessarily simplify the range of functional shapes, missing-data mechanisms, covariance structures, and downstream analyses seen in practice. The EEG application provides an important real-data check, but one application cannot establish performance across biomedical settings. Additional sensitivity analyses and external applications remain part of the ongoing work.
